national.title: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
national.summary: The envoy will also meet with European and NATO allies to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine.
national.body: The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia."We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory seized over the course of the grueling war. Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's land grab would set a dangerous precedent.Witkoff's latest announcement of planned talks at the working level — which generally means discussions among technocrats, not at the senior diplomatic or national leadership level — comes after a rare, localized cease-fire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson ended on Sunday. national.summary: All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, while 36 states will be electing governors.
national.body: In dueling rallies the night before Election Day, the candidates for Texas' Senate seat expressed optimism about one of the closest — and most expensive — races of 2026. Speaking to supporters at a restaurant in Allen, Texas, Republican Ken Paxton noted that most polls show the race is "going to come down to the wire." Paxton highlighted Democrat James Talarico's partisan loyalties, noting the race could decide which party controls the Senate. He accused Talarico of being a tax-and-spend progressive and — fighting words for Texas — a vegan. He told the crowd: "Texas has never been this close to slipping away." "I'm not asking you to imagine what I'd do as your U.S. senator. I'm asking you to look at my record, look at what we've already accomplished and then compare that to James Talarico," Paxton said. At his own concert-style rally in Austin, Talarico predicted that "we are going to shock the nation." His speech was riddled with references to the TV show "Friday Night Lights" and its come-from-behind storylines — nodding to the fact that no Democrat has won statewide in Texas in decades. Talarico railed against "corrupt tariffs," the "corrupt war in the Middle East" and the hundreds of millions of dollars that Elon Musk has poured into the race to aid Paxton. "We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis," he said, calling Paxton "the embodiment of this corrupt system."

national.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
national.summary: US officials described the attacks on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
national.body:
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."

He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.

national.summary: President Trump held an event Monday at the Washington, D.C., Reflecting Pool, while Michigan Democrats assess the fallout from a cross-party endorsement.
national.body:
Follow election updates for Tuesday, Nov. 3, here. See earlier coverage below.

President Trump piled more criticism onto Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed early Tuesday, accusing him of hating Jewish, Black and white people.

"Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks. Don't feel bad, he also Hates Whites," Mr. Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform.

The president said "only fools" would vote for El-Sayed, whom he claimed would "100% do you in!"

The battle for the U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, which could prove decisive in the race to control the Senate, has been contentious. A late surprise endorsement by Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens' of Rogers over her party colleague last week shook up the race, and, according to Stevens' House colleague Rep. Debbie Dingell, it is having the opposite effect of what Stevens intended, "galvanizing many communities" behind El-Sayed.

The balance of power in Washington, D.C., could be tipped by a handful of Senate seats. One of the most competitive races on the ballot is in Maine, where incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins is being challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson.

Voters in Maine, including Norm Belanger, know their vote could impact the rest of the country. He and his wife Elizabeth typically vote for a person over a party, but on Tuesday, they're deciding to unseat the incumbent.

"Troy Jackson doesn't excite me. He would not have been my choice for the Democratic candidate," Belanger said. "On the other hand, I think he's the best choice of the two."

national.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
national.summary: The tech giant reports strong sales but admits "constraints" are affecting supplies of the iPhone Duo.
national.body:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.

The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.

The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".

Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.

Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.

It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen .

Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.

As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.

national.title: Death toll hits 29 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with 48 still missing
national.summary: Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, President Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections.
national.body:
In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, rescuers evacuate a wounded civilian from a residential building after Russian air attack in Dnipro, Ukraine, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Ukrainian Emergency Service/via AP hide caption

KYIV, Ukraine — The death toll from a Russian attack in southern Ukraine on a site where people had gathered to receive humanitarian aid rose to 29 on Tuesday, with 48 still missing, as a wave of overnight strikes targeted power plants across the country, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people.

Dozens of rescuers and volunteers continued to search the cratered blast site of a destroyed aid facility and shelter in Komyushuvakha, a village in Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region, hoping to find missing residents alive under the rubble. Instead, more bodies were pulled out and carried away in white plastic sheeting.

"The scale of the tragedy is terrifying," Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region's military administration, wrote in an online post. "This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war."

A woman and her cat take shelter from a Russian drone and missile attack, in a metro station, now used as a bomb shelter, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Danylo Antoniuk/AP hide caption

Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections.

"The Russians think America won't notice this signal of theirs," he said. "But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes."

Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia where Russian bunker-busting bombs, filled with nearly 1.5 tons of explosives, were used in Monday's attack.

national.title: Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go
national.summary: As polls close on Election Day and results start rolling in, these are some of the House races that will help explain how the midterms are unfolding.
national.body:
Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House on Tuesday. If they do, will their majority be built upon a blue wave or a tiny trickle? A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.

Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress , and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.

So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:

The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 5th Congressional District ( KY-06 ) and Indiana's 5th ( IN-5 ), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.

Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.

Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.

Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.

In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07 , where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10 , where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.

national.title: Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
national.summary: Nintendo's new Ocarina of Time remake enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.
national.body:
Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber. Nintendo hide caption

With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.

Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.

Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.

Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.

In one of the game's most poignant scenes, kid Link answers to the call to adventure, leaving his friend Saria and the Kokiri Forest they called home. Nintendo hide caption

I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring , where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).

You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom . It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.

national.title: Why some key races won't be decided on election night
national.summary: Experts expect some politicians on Tuesday night to claim the 2026 elections are rigged, but here's why that's not the case — and why it may be a while before some races are called.
national.body: Washington — Control of the House and Senate may not be immediately clear on election night, and some of the 2026 midterm election calls will take longer than others. But that's not unusual or an indication of fraud, as some candidates may claim.As the nation watches to see how the elections unfold on Tuesday night, election experts advise voters against listening to politicians who cry foul without offering evidence of fraud as ballots are being cast or counted. Many key races will be close. And when they're close, the results are likely to come later. David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research and a CBS News contributor, says he has some doubts about whether Americans will even know who controls the House or Senate on election night. "If we do, then there's a very big wave going on," Becker said.Candidates "who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it"Becker says there is a type of candidate who's likely to complain early and often about the integrity of the election."It's almost certain that the candidates who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it, trying to fill that vacuum," Becker said, adding that he believes President Trump "will probably spread lies and disinformation about the election on election night because he did it in 2020."When the president was asked last week if he would accept the results of the midterms, whatever the outcome, he responded, "I will if they're honest elections." national.summary: Prosecutors in Lindsay Clancy's case say they plan to have her stand trial a second time, with the judge leaning toward a possible March retrial.
national.body: Prosecutors in Lindsay Clancy's case said Monday they plan to have her stand trial a second time for the murders of her three children, with the judge leaning toward a possible March retrial. What isn't known yet is what charges Clancy would face.In her first trial, Clancy's attorney admitted she killed 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023, but she pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington said Clancy was not criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.Prosecutors said Clancy knew right from wrong and planned to strangle her children. The trial ended with a hung jury on Sept. 4.At a hearing later in September, Reddington then argued that there's "no evidence" Clancy admitted to killing her children. However, in a civil lawsuit, Clancy's lawyers say she admitted to killing them.Will Lindsay Clancy stand trial again? At a hearing in Plymouth Superior Court Monday, prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said for the first time that Clancy will likely stand trial again, though it is not yet known what she would be charged with."This would be a retrial," Sprague said, adding that the prosecution has not yet decided "how that will look."Sprague told Judge William Sullivan she did not want to set a trial date until he ruled on outstanding motions in the case.Reddington took issue with the delay and said he wants to know what charges his client will face. The defense attorney said that the "elephant in the room" is Sullivan's approaching retirement. Reddington said he wants Sullivan to be the trial judge."Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge or no charge?" Reddington said, saying the prosecution should not have to wait for rulings to make a decision on charges. "They don't need to wait for that to determine if they're going to take a run on her again on first-degree. I have to know logistically if it's going to be triple homicide first-degree, or something else."If prosecutors decide to retry Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, she would then have the option to decide between a jury trial or a judge deciding her fate."I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year, or two, or three. national.title: Three scenarios for how the US midterm results could unfold
national.summary: Democratic wave or Republican resilience? Here are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.
national.body:
North America correspondent Published 1 hour ago After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.

According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.

In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.

Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in and what it could mean for the country.

If history is any guide, midterm elections tend to favour of the out-of-power party.

Add in what polls suggest is a historically unpopular president, a war with Iran that has driven up consumer costs and some controversial policies - like aggressive immigration enforcement and support for data centre construction - and you have the conditions for a so-called electoral wave.

In this first scenario, a huge wave is exactly what happens.

Democrats could not only take control of the House of Representatives but far surpass the 218 seats needed for a majority. They may win not only the dozen or so races that election analysts rate as too-close-to-call, they could also flip some seats in more solidly conservative terrain.

national.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
national.summary: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.

He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.

The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

In a letter to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump said Pretoria's actions on international security and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to Washington risked undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.

He also accused South Africa of maintaining significant barriers to American trade and investment, including restrictions affecting agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections and intellectual property.

"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

Millions of Americans are deciding the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.

A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.

Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.

There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report , external .

Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.

This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.

The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.

national.title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
national.summary: Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - died after the plane nosedived.
national.body:
Investigators believe parts of a private jet which crashed in Florida and killed all nine on board may have broken off in the air.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.

A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died on Sunday.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation, but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to a huge crater on the road which was formed by the jet in Palm Beach.

The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time.

"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.

The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, was partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.

Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.

national.title: How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election
national.summary: Race calls are a critical part of election night and NPR partners with the Associated Press to make those calls. Here's how we do it.
national.body:
Voters are voting, ballots are being counted and results are starting to come in for 435 House races, 35 Senate races and 36 gubernatorial contests as well as ballot measures and thousands of state legislative seats. But how will NPR call races on election night? Determining a winner in any of the many races across the country is a big job. That's why NPR partners with the Associated Press — and has for many years — to ensure that races are called accurately.

The Associated Press has been calling races since 1848 and even now, nearly 180 years later, the process for making those calls is pretty simple. Here's how the AP explains its race calling process:

Race callers collaborate with analysts who focus on statewide races, such as those for U.S. Senate and governor, and elections for the U.S. House of Representatives. The decision editors on AP's Decision Team sign off on every race call for president, U.S. Senate and governor, as well as races of significance for U.S. House.

Together, they are looking at far more than just the overall vote totals. They study the incoming vote county by county. In states where the information is available, they look at the vote by type of ballot: cast in person at polling places, or in advance by mail or in person. They are also in constant contact with AP's vote count team, in search of the latest information about what's been counted so far and how many ballots may still be left to count.

Once AP has an idea of how many ballots are outstanding versus how many have been counted, their staff can start to tabulate the likelihood of a certain winner being victorious in a certain contest based on a lot of different factors: where the ballots that are outstanding are coming from, what the makeup of those communities looks like and even, how the individual chose to vote.

For NPR's part, once the AP calls a race, we will alert our broadcast and digital audiences on air as part of special coverage and online through digital stories. We also ensure that our hundreds of member stations also have access to that information. We will use AP's data to populate our election results pages so viewers can keep track, in real time.

But sometimes, races might be called without all — or even most — of the vote counted. How is that possible?

The Associated Press explained in 2024 that it uses that same calculation of ballots, external factors and other data to inform its decisions.

national.title: From 'model minority' to target, anti-Indian hate on the rise
national.summary: A massacre allegedly targeting Hindu Americans was recently thwarted, but researchers say it helps to illustrate a growing and increasingly mainstream hate directed at South Asians in the U.S.
national.body:
A security vehicle is parked outside of Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Ill., on Oct. 15, 2026. Laura Bargfeld/AP hide caption

A 19-year-old man's alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago last month is drawing attention to a recent and steep rise in anti-South Asian and anti-Hindu hate. Police in Palatine, Ill., announced that on Oct. 11, a college student and Taco Bell cashier named Alexandros Paporakis tried to carry out the attack at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Ill., roughly 40 miles west of Chicago. They said the plot was averted by a jammed gun.

"Something of this scale … has not been directed at South Asians before," said Rohit Chopra, professor of communications at Santa Clara University and visiting fellow at the Center for South Asia at Stanford University.

Two decades ago, the predominant narrative about Indian immigrants to the U.S. was glowing, describing the relatively small population as a " model minority ." But Chopra says that over the last four years, a combination of growing anti-immigrant populism, economic anxiety and rising political visibility have dramatically changed the script. Today, he said, online and political discourse more often depict Indian Americans and a broader community of people of South Asian descent in conspiracist, degrading and dehumanizing ways.

"It's become a question of who is American, and deliberately trying to keep the Hindu- and Indian-American community out of those conversations entirely with these sort of preconceived notions and bias against the community," said Prasiddha Sudhakar, a board member of the Network Contagion Research Institute. Sudhakar was formerly a researcher at the NCRI who coauthored some of that organization's reports on the topic.

Most concerning, said Sudhakar and Chopra, is that the toxic online rhetoric they have documented has moved from fringe social media platforms to mainstream ones in a short period of time. And, they said, they see strong connections between online hate and offline violence.

"It didn't start off as mainstream, maybe even like a year or a few years ago. You still saw it on the internet," Sudhakar said. "But what has actually become more important now is that this is reaching many different parts of society in a scale that we've never seen before."

Paporakis has been charged in Illinois with making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a rifle, both felonies. Police said his coworkers called to report the attempted massacre. One of them, according to an affidavit filed by a Cook County assistant state attorney, had spoken by phone with the defendant shortly after the attempted attack. The affidavit further states that Paporakis had also sent that coworker messages, including an eight-page document he had written outlining his motivation for the alleged plot.

Maine's Senate election pits incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins against Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

Collins, first elected in 1996, is seeking a sixth term. She's the only Republican senator from a state Vice President Kamala Harris won in the 2024 presidential election, and she has a long record of outperforming her party, winning by nine points in 2020 when polls showed her losing.

Oyster farmer Graham Platner won the Democratic primary by a landslide in June despite a campaign troubled by controversies, but dropped out of the race a month later after sexual assault allegations emerged. A party convention then chose Jackson, a former logger whose campaign has centered on working-class economics.

national.title: Live Results: Georgia governor midterm election
national.summary: Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson and Democratic former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms are competing to succeed Gov. Brian Kemp.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Georgia Democrat Jon Ossoff is defending his Senate seat Tuesday in one of the nation's marquee races, while Republicans try to hold onto the governor's mansion after two terms under departing GOP Gov. Brian Kemp.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Ossoff is the only Democratic senator seeking reelection in a state President Donald Trump carried in 2024. The seat would be a top prize for Republicans looking to offset possible losses in a midterm environment where the president's party typically loses seats. Republicans can afford to lose no more than three of their 53 Senate seats and still maintain control with Vice President JD Vance casting tiebreaking votes.

Once thought out of reach for Democrats, control of the Senate is increasingly in play as Republican candidates in key contests lose support over disapproval of Trump's handling of high prices and the war in Iran. The Georgia races have drawn Trump to GOP rallies in Dalton and Perry and former President Barack Obama to Atlanta.

Two-term Rep. Mike Collins, from the conservative 10th Congressional District along the South Carolina border, was the top vote-getter in the five-candidate May 19 primary and then won the Republican nomination outright in a June 16 runoff against former University of Tennessee football coach Derek Dooley, 56% to 45%. Trump endorsed Collins for the runoff, while Kemp backed Dooley.

Ossoff, who was unopposed in the Democratic primary, has eclipsed the Collins campaign in fundraising and spending. Ossoff has raised about $137 million as of Oct. 14, compared to about $11 million for Collins. Collins has received help from outside groups such as Republican Senate Leader John Thune's Senate Leadership Fund PAC, but outside groups supporting Ossoff have far outspent those supporting Collins.

In the governor's race, Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson and Democratic former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms are competing to succeed Kemp. Jackson received 53% of the June runoff vote, defeating Trump's pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.

Bottoms clinched the Democratic nomination in the May primary, receiving 56% of the vote in a field of seven.

national.title: Live Results: Alaska Senate midterm election
national.summary: Voters in Alaska are deciding between incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
national.body:
Voters in Alaska are deciding between incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola in the state's closely watched Senate race.

Sullivan, a two-term senator, is backed by President Donald Trump and Sen. Lisa Murkowski.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

Peltola, who represented Alaska in the House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025 and narrowly lost reelection in 2024, entered the race in January at Senate Democrats' urging and is running on affordability. Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election voting rules, which helped Peltola win in 2022, remain in place.

On Oct. 22, at Trump's urging, the Department of Justice sued Alaska's Division of Elections in federal court, asking a judge to block certification of the Senate race if Peltola narrowly wins. The suit accused a third candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, of running with the intention of misleading and confusing the Republican senator's supporters, which the newcomer Sullivan denies. A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit on Sunday.

The New York Times reported that Democrats and Peltola's campaign were involved in recruiting candidates named Dan Sullivan to run. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation and Peltola has denied knowledge of the recruitment efforts.

local.title: Retreat for military spouses combines wellness, support, and fellowship
local.summary: The Healing Haven Wellness Retreat is a free daylong event designed to prioritize the health and wellbeing of military spouses.
local.body:
The New York state veteran's services department is bringing military spouses together for a day of self-care, emotional support, and fellowship.

The inaugural Healing Haven for Military Spouses retreat is a free daylong event that will offer wellness activities, stress reduction workshops, and access to resources and support services for military families.

"We want military spouses to know that they can and should take this time for themselves," said Benjamin Pomerance, deputy counsel for the state Department of Veterans' Services.

Pomerance and his team of wellness experts, including Stress Is Gone with Brett Cotter, are putting together this inaugural getaway as an extension of the Healing Haven for Military Spouses virtual program.

The program, which started in December 2025, Pomerance said offers a safe space where military spouses can "gather in community with each other in a professionally facilitated manner"

"When someone is serving in military uniform, that entire family is serving with them," Pomerance said. "There's just something powerful of being in community with people who have had experiences that are similar to yours, who can talk the same language, so to speak."

Military spouses play a vital yet often undervalued role in supporting those who serve, officials said. Loved ones must navigate deployments, frequent uprooting, adjusting to a one-parent household, and supporting partners who are transitioning back to civilian life.

"The challenges in some ways can be just as great after they come back home and everybody's dealing with the newness of that experience," said Laura Heltz, executive director of the Veterans Outreach Center in Rochester. "A lot of times the service member wants to sort of shield the spouse from some of those issues."

local.body:
Patricia M. (Danforth) Babcock, 82, of Fredonia, passed away Sunday morning, November 1, 2026 at the Chautauqua Nursing and Rehab Center. She was born in Dunkirk on December 31, 1943, she was the wife of Robert R. Babcock II, and daughter of the late Byron and Bernice (Kraiger) Danforth.

A lifelong resident of Dunkirk and Fredonia, Patricia graduated from Dunkirk High School.

Patricia was a loving wife, and mother who devoted much of her life to caring for her family. Over the years, she worked in food service, including positions in the cafeteria at Niagara Mohawk and at the Bomber House. She also took great pride in her role as a homemaker.

Patricia enjoyed working with ceramics and spending time tending to her flower garden. She was an active member of St. John's Church, where she enjoyed being involved in her church community. Patricia will be remembered for her love and devotion to her family and the care she showed to those around her.

Patricia is survived by her loving husband of 56 years, Robert Babcock II, her sons, Sean Morrison, John (Jami) Babcock, Patrick (Margaret) Babcock, Robert (Michelle) Babcock III, and Steven Babcock; five grandchildren and her siblings, John (Lori) Danforth and Barbara Adamczak.

In addition to her parents, she is preceded in death by her grandson, Jared Babcock.

Relatives and friends are welcome to attend Calling Hours on Wednesday, November 4, 2026 from 2-4 p.m. and 6-8 p.m. at the McGraw-Kowal Funeral Home, 736 Central Avenue, Dunkirk, NY. Prayer services will begin at 6 p.m. Interment will be held privately in Willowbrook Park Cemetery. Arrangements are by R. Michael Mackowiak III; McGraw-Kowal Funeral Home. Share condolences at, www.mcgrawkowalfuneralhome.com.

local.summary: The newest edition of a plan to revamp Wright Park Beach and Lakefront Boulevard moves the beach slightly west and keeps the road open. The city of Dunkirk Planning and Development Department held a joint online meeting with the Buffalo Niagara Waterkeeper organization Tuesday to describe the latest
local.body:
The newest edition of a plan to revamp Wright Park Beach and Lakefront Boulevard moves the beach slightly west and keeps the road open.

The city of Dunkirk Planning and Development Department held a joint online meeting with the Buffalo Niagara Waterkeeper organization Tuesday to describe the latest plan.

"This has been a fantastic project that has helped some of the best coastal engineers of the country look at Wright Park and Lakefront Boulevard as a system," city Planning and Development Director Vince DeJoy said.

"It’s been a fabulous team effort and it doesn't end here," he said. The plan discussed Tuesday "represents 30% (of the) design and engineering" for the improvement project. "We have submitted a grant application to get to a full design and engineering, to allow us to then apply for grant funding for implementation," he said.

DeJoy noted that he will be moving to North Carolina shortly, but talked up his deputy director EJ Hayes, stating that Hayes should be able to fill his shoes seamlessly on the project.

The presentation listed the following big-picture objectives for the project:

-- Emphasize nature-based strategies, habitat preservation and creation.

-- Protect critical infrastructure along Lakefront Boulevard, along with the nearby wastewater treatment plant.

local.body:
OBSERVER Photo by Braden Carmen Fredonia seniors Elly Saunders (1) and Londyn Wilmot (8) celebrate with Alyse Bugaj (7) and their teammates after a point during Monday’s Section VI Class B2 semifinal girls volleyball game against Springville Griffith at Fredonia High School.

OBSERVER Photo by Braden Carmen Fredonia libero Sophia Pagan returns a serve during a Section VI Class B2 semifinal girls volleyball game on Monday at Fredonia High School.

FREDONIA -- Two years ago, the Fredonia 'Billies were Section VI champions. This year, they will play for that honor again, and their coach believes they deserve the crown as much as any team she has ever coached.

"I haven't had a team this unified, where everyone wants this, everyone is willing to put in what it takes to get there," Fredonia head coach Amanda Krakowiak said. "It's a dream to have a team like this. They have the heart and they really, really want this. It's just amazing to work with a group of girls like that."

Fredonia claimed its spot back in the sectional title game with a victory over the Springville Griffith Griffins 25-8, 25-10, a 25-12 in Monday's Class B2 semifinal volleyball match at Fredonia High School.

"We have a really good connection. Getting these big wins like this one is really amazing, to be able to do that with everyone we've grown so close with over the years," said Fredonia senior Elly Saunders.

The 'Billies essentially brought back the same team it had a year ago. But the story of this year's team dates back to two years ago when the 'Billies won the sectional championship with a win over Southwestern, then with a win over Depew in the Class B crossover.

"One of the things I had preached to that team a couple years ago was, 'You guys are paving the path for the future, creating this opportunity for the future teams here at Fredonia. They are going to look up to you and they are going to see that this team was able to do it,'" Krakowiak said.

local.title: Portville survives Chautauqua Lake in 5 sets
local.summary: PORTVILLE — The Portville girls volleyball team has won every Section VI Class C volleyball championship since 2014 and the Panthers have claimed the last five New York State Public High School Athletic Association championships. In recent years, Portville has seldom been tested in the sectional pla
local.body:
PORTVILLE -- The Portville girls volleyball team has won every Section VI Class C volleyball championship since 2014 and the Panthers have claimed the last five New York State Public High School Athletic Association championships.

In recent years, Portville has seldom been tested in the sectional playoffs and has cruised to several of its state titles. However, with three losses in the regular season, the Panthers looked beatable to some teams in Class C.

That set the stage for the Section VI Class C semifinals on Monday with No. 1 Portville hosting No. 4 Chautauqua Lake -- which is ranked second in the state, according to the New York State Sportswriters Association -- making for a state-level competition. The undefeated Eagles showed they were right on the level of Portville with a 25-23 win in the first set, but the Panthers hung on in the back-and-forth contest that finished in five sets with the streak staying alive 23-25, 25-22, 22-25, 25-15, 15-13.

"Any time you play Portville there is a lot of hype behind it," Chautauqua Lake head coach Joanne Meadows said. "I think with the team I had this year everybody thought it would be a great match and it was a great match. I really can't ask a lot more from my kids than what they did. We had a couple of times where we made a few mistakes, but it's high school volleyball (and) there is going to be mistakes. I'm very proud of the way they played. It was an awesome match and I think it lived up to what everyone thought it was going to be."

In a rematch of last year's semifinals, Chautauqua Lake showed it was up to the task, unlike last year when the Eagles were quickly swept. Falling behind 20-15, the Eagles were not fazed by the score and seized the momentum at the end of the set with runs of four and three in a 25-23 win.

"I think it absolutely gave us a boost," Meadows said about winning the opening set. "Last year we came here and got absolutely swept and bombed. When they came in this year and took the first set that definitely increased the momentum for us for a little while. Volleyball is such a momentum sport, so that really makes a difference."

The loss was Portville's first in the Section VI playoffs since 2022 when it dropped one set against Eden in the final.

Chautauqua Lake rode that wave into the second set and jumped to a 5-1 lead that included two big kills from freshman Brina Jacobson and an ace by senior setter Karagan Fairbank.

local.body:
The Dunkirk City School District has awarded dozens of bids worth more than $21 million for the next phase of its long-term construction project.

The Dunkirk Board of Education approved the bids for Phase 1.3 of the project at its October meeting. A total of 24 bids were awarded in six areas of work.

District Superintendent Brian Swatland called it "the biggest phase" in the capital project.

The cafeteria and kitchen at the Middle and High School will get renovated. A new connecting corridor and courtyard will be added at the school. The football field, track, and tennis courts are getting refurbished, and new scoreboards are planned.

In addition, air conditioning will be added to district classrooms. Finally, a new "School Based Health Office" will get added.

The capital project already has a visible benefit: Construction is complete on a new Sixth Street entrance and addition.

The 24 bids awarded for Phase 1.3 totaled $21,171,650. They are as follows:

local.body:
Pick a Thanksgiving table, any Thanksgiving table in America, and it’s sure to have a turkey and a grumpy uncle.

Sometimes they are one and the same, stuffed with all the trimmings.

As the midterms are decided, this November will be an especially heated month, right? We the people are so deeply carved down the center. There’s no moderate middle ground.

As the presumptive winners of the House, the Democratic family members get the white meat. The Republicans will have to do with dark. The winner of the Senate gets dibs on pumpkin pie.

Oh, what a feast it will be for starved Democrats, after two long years in the Donald Trump wilderness. It feels like 40, right?

Elon Musk, Trump’s loaded right-hand man, will gobble up leftovers at his knee like a DOGE, but he won’t have a place at the table.

Everything we love, everything we thought we knew about America, is under siege.

Under the usual circumstances, the grumpy uncle could pass with his harsh social comments, his barely disguised racism and his loud voice trumpeting over the younger company.

local.summary: The NYSDEC is moving ahead with the second phase of a multi-year, multi-million-dollar effort to make Zoar Valley safer and more accessible.
local.body: The NYSDEC is moving ahead with the second phase of a multi-year, multi-million-dollar effort to make Zoar Valley safer and more accessible.The work includes significant upgrades to Valentine Flats Trail, the main access point for emergency crews trying to reach the valley floor and Cattaraugus Creek.Plans call for widening and hardening the trail to make it easier for first responders to get down to the water and back out. The improvements are also expected to accommodate utility terrain vehicles, helping emergency crews respond more efficiently.For Marla Walker, the work has special meaning. "The terrain continues to change and that's going to keep going so that they're going to make it safer for everybody."WATCH: Zoar Valley begins next phase of safety upgrades, with major trail work plannedWork is also continuing on the Memorial Trail near the Valentine Flats parking area. local.title: Federal disaster recovery loans available for Buffalo, Northtowns residents hit by September flooding
local.summary: Disaster recovery loans are now available to Northtowns and North Buffalo residents and businesses impacted by September's flash flooding.
local.body: Two months after record rainfall caused flash flooding in North Buffalo, the federal government is in town offering disaster recovery loans to those impacted.The U.S. Small Business Administration is offering low-interest loans to those affected and has opened a temporary field office at the Ellwood Volunteer Firehouse in the Town of Tonawanda, where neighbors can get guidance on how to apply."We are here to assist all the people who suffered damage in the recent storms," said Carlos Narvaez of the Small Business Administration.The loans are open to property owners, renters, non profit organizations and small businesses impacted by the flooding, with interest rates starting at 3% according to Narvaez.Days after the floods, I spoke to Justin Hofschneider, owner of small business Wine on Hertel. His basement was flooded with approximately 2ft of water on Sept. 3. I caught up with him on Monday to see what he makes of the loans. "Truthfully, it's not a good fit for me and my business," Hofschneider said.WATCH: Federal disaster recovery loans available for Buffalo, Northtowns residents hit by September floodingHe told me he does not want to take on debt after already paying for the cleanup."I was truly hoping for grants because I lost $20,000 worth of things and I just spent the last two months getting right again," Hofschneider said.Those interested in applying can head to the temporary field office at Ellwood Volunteer Fire Department at 1000 Englewood Avenue, or apply at sba.gov/disaster. The field office is open through November 16. The deadline to apply is December 18.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

local.title: 'People keep dying': Second crash in 11 days at Lockport intersection
local.summary: Neighbors who live near the intersection of Bartz and Rapids roads in the Town of Lockport are calling for safety changes after two people were killed in separate crashes there last month.
local.body: Neighbors who live near the intersection of Bartz and Rapids roads in the Town of Lockport are calling for safety changes after two people were killed in separate crashes there last month.The most recent crash happened Friday and claimed the life of a 27-year-old mother of two young children.Henry Kamens has lived on Bartz Road for nearly 40 years and said he has seen crash after crash at the intersection."I don't know what they have to do," Kamens said. "People keep dying."Another fatal crash happened Oct. 19. In that case, Kamens said a Jeep stopped at the stop sign on Bartz Road and then drove into the path of a cement truck traveling on Rapids Road.At the intersection, Crosby Road becomes Bartz Road. Drivers traveling on Bartz and Crosby have a stop sign, while traffic on Rapids Road does not.Kamens believes some drivers mistakenly think the intersection is a four-way stop."They think it's a four-way stop," Kamens said. "They just look, you know.... they stop and they just go. They don't really think that the traffic is coming, even though we have signs up there."Kamens said he'd like to see additional traffic controls installed."I think they should put either a signal in or a four-way stop," he said.Town of Lockport Supervisor Mark Crocker said the NYS Department of Transportation has previously determined there was not enough traffic at the intersection to warrant a traffic signal.WATCH: 'People keep dying': Second crash in 11 days at Lockport intersectionCrocker also said Niagara County recently spent $6 million on Rapids Road, including regrading the slope of the roadway in an effort to improve visibility at the intersection.They've also put up signs ahead of the stop signs indicating that the cross traffic doesn't have a stop sign. They've also installed extra large stop sighs at the intersection.Crocker said it would be up to Niagara County to install stop signs for traffic on Rapids Road, a change he supports.7 News also reached out to Niagara County about the intersection.Join the Niagara County Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.

local.title: Summit Center opens seventh STEPS location in East Amherst
local.summary: The new community-based day habilitation hub helps adults with autism and other developmental disabilities build everyday skills, friendships and independence.
local.body: The Summit Center is expanding its community-based day habilitation program with the opening of its seventh STEPS location, creating more opportunities for adults with autism and other developmental disabilities to build skills and stay connected to their communities.STEPS, which stands for Success Through Engagement and Positive Supports, serves adults ages 21 and older who need continued support after aging out of the school system.Unlike traditional day programs, STEPS is designed to operate "without walls." Participants spend time in their communities taking part in recreational activities, volunteering and learning everyday skills.For participant William Salamon, that includes trips to the grocery store, where he and other participants recently worked together to plan a Thanksgiving meal.From choosing ingredients to comparing prices and budgeting, the outing provides an opportunity to practice skills that can translate into everyday independence."Budgeting. That's the key word here. Budgeting," Salamon said.The program also gives participants opportunities to build friendships and work toward individual goals. Salamon said his next goal is to move into a group home, and he's already on a waiting list.WATCH: Summit Center opens seventh STEPS location in East AmherstWendy Loverme, director of Community and Adult Services at The Summit Center, said the program was created to help fill the gap in services for adults after high school.Participants help choose activities based on their interests and goals. Outings can include shopping, bowling, mall walks and volunteer opportunities. Staff members provide support and assistance as needed.The newest STEPS hub is located in a renovated home on Transit Road in East Amherst. The property was donated to The Summit Center by West Herr Auto Group. The location opened Sept. 9 and is expected to grow to serve 12 participants.The Summit Center has seven STEPS locations throughout Western New York, with each hub generally serving individuals who live within a 10-mile radius. local.title: Union Road bridge in West Seneca fully reopens after months of construction
local.summary: After months of traffic disruptions and a pause in work to protect a threatened fish species, the Union Road bridge over Cazenovia Creek in West Seneca has fully reopened.
local.body: After months of traffic disruptions and a pause in work to protect a threatened fish species, the Union Road bridge over Cazenovia Creek in West Seneca has fully reopened.The New York State Department of Transportation confirmed the bridge is now open to traffic, marking the substantial completion of a project designed to protect the structure's long-term safety and integrity.The project faced several setbacks, including structural issues, weather and environmental restrictions.Earlier this year, construction crews were unable to perform work in the creek between May 1 and June 30 because of state environmental protections for the bigeye chub, a threatened fish species found only in Western New York.At the time, the DOT said work on the bridge's substructure would resume July 1, with the overall project expected to be completed by the end of 2026.The extended construction period also frustrated nearby businesses and motorists.Now, the bridge is fully reopened, although construction crews still have some work to finish.WATCH: Union Road bridge in West Seneca fully reopens after months of constructionThe DOT says finishing work will continue through the remainder of the year, with occasional single-lane closures anticipated over the next several weeks.In a statement, the department acknowledged the disruption the project caused."The Department of Transportation recognizes the significant impact construction has had on motorists and the West Seneca community, and we appreciate the public's patience throughout construction," A NYSDOT spokesperson said.The department has not provided a specific date for when all remaining work will be completed.

local.title: Veterans Day Parade is Saturday
local.summary: It will conclude with a ceremony at the Greater Rochester Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Gary Beikirch Park on South Avenue.
local.body:
Monroe County's fifth annual Veterans Day Parade is scheduled to start at 10:30 a.m. Saturday from South Goodman and Highland avenues.

From there, the parade will proceed up Highland Avenue to the Greater Rochester Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Gary Beikirch Park on South Avenue, where it will conclude with a ceremony, according to a news release from Monroe County.

The parade will include musical marching units, veterans’ service organizations, law enforcement representatives, military-style vehicles, active-duty service members, and groups representing veterans of all eras and military branches, the county said.

State Senate Minority Leader Robert Ortt, a Republican from North Tonawanda whose district includes Sweden and Ogden, will be the grand marshal. Ortt is a decorated veteran of the U.S. Army National Guard who enlisted in response to the Sept. 11 attacks.

local.title: Wells College finds new buyer for historic campus
local.summary: A Chicago developer made a $10 million cash offer that the college accepted last week. The goal is to close in February 2027.
local.body:
A Chicago-based real estate developer has signed a purchase agreement to buy the former Wells College campus in Aurora with plans for a senior living community.

"For now we're still negotiating," said developer Paul Warshauer, who made a $10 million cash offer and signed the agreement last Thursday. "We're in, basically, the due diligence period, the examination period.

"We need to really make sure that the numbers work," he continued, "before we, you know, sign."

The plan is to renovate roughly half the 113-acre scenic property along Cayuga Lake for independent and assisted living as well as memory care units. The athletic facilities would be grouped for another youth or community sports operator, he said. And the remaining buildings could again be utilized for an unspecified educational purpose, possibly an existing university's satellite campus.

"For the record, we have no desire at this time to demolish any of the buildings," said Warshauer, who specializes in reuse of historic properties. "We're going to keep them all."

The college shut down in June 2024 . And what seemingly was the most promising offer —a $12.5 million bid from The Hiawatha Institute for Indigenous Knowledge, which planned to open an accredited university dedicated to Indigenous studies — fell through. The institute sued the college over the botched transaction. There is a court hearing set for December to decide whether that case should be dismissed.

Warshauer was an early partner with Hiawatha Institute, "until I realized that they didn't have any money," he said. Messages left with the institute on Monday were not immediately returned.

The college recently went back out to bid, seeking interested buyers and saying it was open to selling off the campus piece by piece . But Warshauer said the college was smart not to do so, adding: "Now it just takes a vision to put all the pieces together, and that's what we're doing."

entertainment.title: Cinemark Posts Sharply Higher Third-Quarter Results Amid Hollywood Box Office Rebound
entertainment.summary: The movie theater giant, led by CEO Sean Gamble, saw concession and admissions revenues rise from year-earlier levels.
entertainment.body:
Exhibition giant Cinemark Holdings on Tuesday unveiled its third-quarter financial results, posting higher revenue and earnings compared to a year ago.

The big reveal was how a strong movie slate allowed the exhibition giant to sustain gains from this summer’s Hollywood box office rebound into its latest financial quarter. Cinemark saw total revenue rise to $1.05 billion, against a year-earlier $857.5 million in the same period of 2025.

Admissions revenue during the latest quarter was $530.8 million, up from a year-earlier $427.7 million, with attendance of 63.7 million customers. And concession revenue came to $413.9 million, against $336.7 million in the same period of 2025. Related Stories Movies British Independent Film Awards: 'Elsinore' Leads Nominations With 12 Lifestyle Marilyn Monroe, Audrey Hepburn, PÖFF Garments Bring the Glitz to New Fashion Museum Near Tallinn

The latest financial results for Cinemark for the three months to Sept. 30, 2026 came amid a summer box office rebound for Hollywood titles at the local multiplex that has lifted the hopes of major studios and exhibitors coming out of the pandemic era.

Net income at Cinemark for the third quarter came to $124.2 million, rising from a year-earlier $50.5 million. The company’s third-quarter adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), another profitability metric, rose to $276.6 million, compared to a year-earlier $177.6 million.

Sean Gamble, Cinemark’s president and CEO, in a statement that accompanied the firm’s latest financial results, said: “Our ability to translate positive box office momentum from a compelling slate of summer releases into consistent, meaningful earnings growth reflects the strength of our operating model, the effectiveness of our team and the sustained impact of our strategic initiatives.”

entertainment.title: ABC News Drops New Episode of ‘The Dropout’ That Tackles ‘You Can See Everything’
entertainment.summary: The podcast that inspired the Hulu series last released a new episode in 2022, but listenership has surged following the success of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary film.
entertainment.body:
Surprise true crime fans and Elizabeth Holmes obsessives: There’s a new episode of The Dropout to chew on.

The ABC News podcast that inspired the Emmy-winning Hulu series released a special bonus episode Tuesday, one that tackles the stunning success of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary film You Can See Everything , from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

Without delving into spoiler territory, the film addresses The Dropout TV series, at one point having Holmes watch some of it with Fielder in her home. Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything,' 'Clayface' Fighting for No. 1 in Quiet Halloween Weekend SCAD Savannah Film Festival Nathan Fielder Addresses Unconventional Doc Techniques in 'You Can See Everything' as Academy Doc Branch Members Weigh In (Exclusive)

The Dropout podcast debuted in 2019, and a second season ran in 2021, with some bonus episodes released in 2022, coinciding with the Amanda Seyfried-starring Hulu series it inspired. As with those earlier episodes, the new episode is led by Rebecca Jarvis, ABC News chief business, technology and economics correspondent and Good Morning America contributing anchor, who created the initial podcast and was a producer on the Hulu series.

The episode includes a sit-down with Theranos whistleblower Erika Cheung, in part to get her reaction to the film.

The Dropout podcast has seen a resurgence since the film’s release, with ABC saying that the show has seen a “2500 percent increase in plays across Spotify and Apple” in the second week since the film’s release. Now ABC is betting that a new episode can keep that momentum going.

entertainment.body:
Logo text With less than 24 hours until Election Day, and a potential control flip of Congress , late-night hosts didn’t waste any time on Monday taking jabs at those making headlines heading into the midterms, namely Donald Trump and former Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens.

On The Daily Show , Jon Stewart seemed quite confused why Trump — who has been on the campaign trail for the past month, advocating for Republican candidates across the U.S. — used his final pre-election speech to talk about the controversial renovations he made to the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. Related Stories News Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell Set for Kennedy Center Honors Business Inside CNN's Tech-Forward Midterm Election Set

“That was the president of the United States, on the day before the midterms, choosing to make a speech at the reflecting pool to talk about the reflecting pool. No symbolism, no metaphors, just straight-up pool maintenance. That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech, if you will,” the host said, drawing laughter from his live audience.

After calling the president’s priorities “badly misplaced,” Stewart noted that “Democrats appear in position for a wave election” in the U.S. House and Senate “as long as the remaining couple of days before the election are bombshellless, drama-free, non-earthquakey.”

Welp… it looks like Michigan didn’t get that memo. Stevens caused quite the shakeup over the weekend with her shocking endorsement of GOP candidate Mike Rogers for Senate after breaking with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“We all knew there was drama in Michigan when Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in a contentious primary for the Democratic nomination, but Stevens has always been very clear as to their shared goal of defeating Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers,” Stewart said, before clips played of Stevens repeatedly criticizing the GOP candidate.

“What the fuck happened? This is like the most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen,” the host quipped.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! , Kimmel kicked off his overtly political monologue with a reference to Trump and his continued legal woes, particularly in relation to the dead sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. “Remember that birthday card Trump didn’t draw for Jeffrey Epstein on his 50th birthday? This is why Donald Trump sued The Wall Street Journal for $10 billion for claiming he did draw that card,” said Kimmel. “He’s got a hefty bag full of frivolous lawsuits out there trying to protect himself against the blue wave, which seems to be headed his way tomorrow. Tomorrow is midterm election day.”

entertainment.title: The Chicks Postpone Los Angeles Concert Hours Before Showtime Due to Illness
entertainment.summary: The trio are currently wrapping their Taking the Long Way 20th anniversary tour.
entertainment.body:
The Chicks have have postponed their Los Angeles concert just hours before doors were scheduled to open, citing illness.

The trio announced Monday (Nov. 2) that their show at Hollywood’s Dolby Theatre would no longer go ahead as planned and had been rescheduled for Wednesday (Nov. 4). All previously purchased tickets will remain valid for the new date, while fans who are unable to attend can request refunds from their original point of purchase, according to a statement shared by the group.

The postponed show comes as The Chicks near the end of their Taking the Long Way 20th anniversary tour, a run built around the album that became one of the defining releases of their career. Related Justin Timberlake to Release 4-Part Docuseries That Includes Janet Jackson as a Guest Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan's Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: 'He's a Fighter' Tate McRae's 'Housewife' Scores Second Week at No. 1 on Billboard Global Charts Explore The Chicks See latest videos, charts and news

Released in 2006, Taking the Long Way debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and went on to become a major commercial and critical success. Its most enduring single, “Not Ready to Make Nice,” reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became one of the group’s signature songs.

The album also dominated the 2007 Grammy Awards, with The Chicks winning five trophies, including album of the year. “Not Ready to Make Nice” took home both record of the year and song of the year.

The record arrived after a turbulent period for the group. In 2003, Natalie Maines criticized then-President George W. Bush and the Iraq War during a concert in London, prompting widespread backlash from parts of the country music industry and conservative audiences in the U.S.

Some country radio stations stopped playing the group’s music, while protests and boycotts followed.

That fallout became a major thematic thread on Taking the Long Way , particularly on “Not Ready to Make Nice,” where The Chicks directly addressed the pressure to apologize and their decision not to back down.

entertainment.title: Here’s Why the My Chemical Romance Lawsuit Really Ended, According to the Band’s Manager
entertainment.summary: Court filings reveal a new explanation for why the high-profile legal dispute with the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders wrapped up so quickly.
entertainment.body:
My Chemical Romance had always planned to stop using Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders uniforms after just three concerts, and a headline-grabbing lawsuit from the cheer squad played no role in that decision, the band’s manager says in new court filings.

The cheerleaders sued last month , demanding a restraining order after the band’s backup dancers wore look-alike uniforms during shows at the Hollywood Bowl — the grand finale of a dystopian rock opera celebrating the 20th anniversary of the band’s The Black Parade album .

The case ended just days later , reportedly after My Chemical Romance promised not to use the costumes at future shows. But in a sworn statement filed in court Thursday (Oct. 29), the band’s manager, Brian Schechter , said that had always been the plan and was not a response to the lawsuit.

“From the outset, the Finale — with its elaborate sets, full cast, and resolution of the story told during the 2025 and 2026 tours — was planned to be performed only on Oct. 21, 23, and 24, 2026, and on no other date,” Schechter wrote in the Oct. 29 declaration.

“All of these decisions were made nearly a year before I first learned, on Oct. 22, 2026, after the Finale’s first performance, that [the cheerleaders] objected to it,” Schechter wrote. “The Finale was last performed on Oct. 24, 2026, because of those earlier decisions that it was the last performance of that three-part story, not because of any objection by plaintiff.”

In an emailed response to Billboard , Alex Spiro , lead counsel for the Cowboys Cheerleaders, flatly dismissed the idea that the band had already been planning to stop using the uniforms long in advance: “Sure they were,” he writes. “They waved the white flag.”

The band’s attorney did not immediately return a request for comment.

The Black Parade , the band’s 2006 magnum opus, reached the top of the Billboard 200 this week after an anniversary reissue. My Chemical Romance spent the past two years touring ahead of the looming milestone, culminating in the trio of theatrical concerts at the Hollywood Bowl last month. The shows, which told a satirical story about the “United States by Draag,” featured one scene in which the Cowboys Cheerleaders, armed with rifles, engaged in a faux-firefight on stage.
